pr.title: Stop a test chunk that hangs instead of waiting on it forever
pr.head: df41a8ede1bc569668350f79271632ae1244fcac

summary: python3 -m tests is Projector's test runner. It splits the suite into chunks, lists of at most eight tests from one class, and runs each chunk as its own python3 -m unittest process, several at a time.

Before this change, each chunk inherited the runner's stdin, and the runner waited on each chunk with no time limit. Started from a background shell, whose stdin never closes, one test's fake claude script piped its input through cat, and cat waited forever, so the whole run did too. At a terminal or in CI, stdin closes or is empty, so the hang never showed there.
The change fixes both halves, and keeps Ctrl-C working with the new process groups:

• No stdin. Each chunk starts with stdin connected to /dev/null, so a test that reads stdin reads nothing and goes on.
  • A time limit. Each chunk runs in a process group of its own. Past --timeout seconds, 300 by default, the runner kills the whole group, or only the chunk's own process where os.killpg does not exist, as on Windows, and fails the chunk with The chunk ran past 300 seconds and was stopped.
  • Ctrl-C stops the chunks. A chunk in a session of its own no longer receives the SIGINT that Ctrl-C sends the terminal's foreground process group, so when the runner is interrupted, it starts no more chunks and kills the group of each running one itself.

The runner kills the group rather than the chunk's process alone because a process a test started, such as that cat, holds the chunk's output pipes open, and the runner would keep waiting to read them.

groups.title: The runner stops a chunk that hangs
groups.kicker: No stdin for a chunk, and a timeout that kills its whole process group
intro: run starts one chunk. It replaces subprocess.run with a Popen so that on a timeout it can kill the chunk's process group before reading the rest of the output. A process group is the set of processes the chunk and everything it starts belong to; start_new_session=True gives the chunk a group of its own, so os.killpg reaches its children without touching the runner. stop does that kill, and both the timeout and an interrupt use it.

Because a chunk in its own session misses Ctrl-C, run records each live chunk in the module-level running set under running_lock. When main catches KeyboardInterrupt, interrupt cancels the chunks not yet started, sets the interrupted flag, and stops every recorded chunk, then main re-raises.

The tests in tests/test_runner.py drive run directly with a small probe module written to a temporary directory: one probe test pipes stdin through cat, one waits on a sleep 60 child, one sleeps for 60 seconds itself, for the test that removes os.killpg, and one records its sleep 60 child's pid for the interrupt test, which runs the whole runner as a process.

checks.text: The gate passed at this head: claude plugin validate, claude plugin test, git diff --check, and the check CI job, which runs tests.test_runner, the interrupt test included.

files.note: The runner: run starts each chunk with no stdin and a timeout, --timeout SECONDS sets the limit, and main stops the running chunks when it is interrupted.

checks.text: A chunk that starts while an interrupt is being handled is still stopped. run adds its process and reads interrupted under running_lock, and interrupt sets the flag under the same lock before it stops what is recorded, so a chunk either is in the set when interrupt walks it or sees the flag and stops itself. Traced by reading both functions.
communicate raised TimeoutExpired before it reaped the chunk, so the group still exists when stop runs killpg, and the second communicate returns once every process holding the pipes is dead.

Where os.killpg does not exist, as on Windows, the runner kills only the chunk's own process. The chunk still fails, but a process the chunk started that holds its output open keeps the second communicate waiting, as the comment says.
After interrupt, the with ThreadPoolExecutor block's own shutdown still waits for the workers, but each one returns as soon as its killed group closes the output pipes.

files.note: Five tests: a chunk ignores a stdin that never closes, a chunk past its timeout fails along with its children, a chunk past its timeout still fails where os.killpg does not exist, a SIGINT to the runner stops the running chunk and its child, and --help shows --timeout SECONDS.

The developer guide says that a chunk runs with no stdin, that one past --timeout seconds, 300 by default, is stopped and fails, that Ctrl-C stops every running chunk the same way, and lists --timeout among the runner's options.
